--- title: "How Many More Died? Excess Deaths in Greece Since 2015" description: "Weekly deaths in Greece in Eurostat data, against the deaths a normal year would bring: the pandemic, the heatwaves, who died, how Greece compares with the EU, and why fewer people have died since 2024." author: "" --- ## What is this? Counting the deaths of a disease is hard: doctors must decide what each person died of, and countries decide it in different ways. Counting all deaths is easy, and every EU country reports them to Eurostat week by week. The deaths above what a normal week would bring are the **excess deaths**: they include the deaths of the disease that nobody recorded as such, and the deaths that a heatwave or an overwhelmed hospital caused. This story compares the deaths of every week in Greece since 2015 with the deaths a normal year would have brought, and answers seven questions: 1. **How many people die in Greece in a normal week?** 2. **How many more died during the pandemic?** 3. **Which weeks were the worst?** 4. **Does the heat kill too?** 5. **Who died?** 6. **How does Greece compare with the EU?** 7. **What came after the pandemic?** The deaths come from **Eurostat**, the temperatures of Athens from **ERA5-Land**, a reconstruction of the weather of every day by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. Both are downloaded when the page is rendered, so a new render brings in the latest weeks. --- ## Packages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages(c("eurostat","plotly")) library(eurostat) library(plotly) ``` ::: ## The data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # a Eurostat dataset, without its missing values; the time as text: "2024-W05", "2024-05" eurostat_values<-function(id,filters) { x<-get_eurostat(id,filters=filters,time_format="raw",cache=FALSE) result<-as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values),]) result$time<-as.character(result$time) return(result) } # the Monday that an ISO week ("2024-W05") starts on: week 1 is the week with 4 January in it week_monday<-function(time) { january_4<-as.Date(paste0(substr(time,1,4),"-01-04")) result<-january_4-(as.integer(format(january_4,"%u"))-1)+7*(as.integer(substr(time,7,8))-1) return(result) } # deaths in Greece every week since 2015, all ages weekly<-eurostat_values("demo_r_mwk_ts",list(geo="EL",sex="T")) weekly<-weekly[order(weekly$time),c("time","values")] names(weekly)[2]<-"deaths" weekly$year<-as.integer(substr(weekly$time,1,4)) weekly$week<-as.integer(substr(weekly$time,7,8)) weekly$monday<-week_monday(weekly$time) # deaths every week by age, in ten-year groups by_age<-eurostat_values("demo_r_mwk_10",list(geo="EL",sex="T")) # Eurostat's own measure: the deaths of each month against the average of the same month in # 2016-2019, %, for every EU country eurostat_excess<-eurostat_values("demo_mexrt",list(unit="PC")) # the highest temperature of every day in Athens since 2015, from ERA5-Land through Open-Meteo, as # one CSV file: two lines about the point of the grid, an empty line, then the days weather_url<-paste0("https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive", "?latitude=37.98&longitude=23.73&start_date=2015-01-01&end_date=", Sys.Date()-1,"&daily=temperature_2m_max&timezone=Europe%2FAthens", "&models=era5_land&format=csv") weather<-read.csv(text=readLines(weather_url)[-(1:3)],col.names=c("date","tmax")) weather<-weather[!is.na(weather$tmax),] # the last few days are not ready yet weather$time<-format(as.Date(weather$date),"%G-W%V") # the average of the highest temperatures of each week heat<-aggregate(tmax~time,weather,mean) weekly$tmax<-heat$tmax[match(weekly$time,heat$time)] ``` ::: ### The deaths a normal year would bring A normal week has more deaths in winter, when flu and the cold strike, than in summer, and the deaths of a normal year grow slowly as the population gets older. So the expected deaths of each week come from a model of the five years before the pandemic, 2015–2019: each week of the year has its own level, and every year adds the same share to all of them. It is a Poisson regression, the usual model for counts, with a dispersion that is allowed to be larger than Poisson's. The years 53 weeks long count their last week as week 52. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the expected deaths of every week, from the weeks of 2015-2019, and how far a normal week may # stray from them: twice the standard deviation of the model expect<-function(x) { x$season<-factor(pmin(x$week,52)) before<-x[x$year<=2019,] model<-glm(deaths~year+season,family=quasipoisson,data=before) x$expected<-predict(model,newdata=x,type="response") spread<-2*sqrt(summary(model)$dispersion*x$expected) x$low<-x$expected-spread x$high<-x$expected+spread x$excess<-x$deaths-x$expected x$percent<-100*x$excess/x$expected result<-list(weeks=x,growth=100*(exp(coef(model)[["year"]])-1)) return(result) } fitted<-expect(weekly) weekly<-fitted$weeks # the deaths of every year: what was expected, what happened, and the difference years<-data.frame(year=sort(unique(weekly$year))) years$weeks<-as.vector(table(weekly$year)[as.character(years$year)]) years$deaths<-as.vector(tapply(weekly$deaths,weekly$year,sum)) years$expected<-as.vector(tapply(weekly$expected,weekly$year,sum)) years$excess<-years$deaths-years$expected years$percent<-100*years$excess/years$expected at<-function(column,year) { result<-years[[column]][years$year==year] return(result) } pandemic<-years[years$year%in%2020:2022,] last_full<-max(years$year[years$weeks>=52]) # the weeks with the most and the fewest expected deaths in 2019 normal<-weekly[weekly$year==2019,] peak<-normal[which.max(normal$expected),] trough<-normal[which.min(normal$expected),] # the deaths of the last full year against an average year of 2016-2019, % (all 52 weeks long), # and Eurostat's measure for the same year before_average<-mean(years$deaths[years$year%in%2016:2019]) after_change<-100*(at("deaths",last_full)/before_average-1) eurostat_last<-mean(eurostat_excess$values[eurostat_excess$geo=="EL"& substr(eurostat_excess$time,1,4)==last_full]) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} greek_red<-"#d62728" blue<-"#1f77b4" gray<-"#9e9e9e" dark_gray<-"#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes and the labels # the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout chart<-function(p,title,source,y_title="",y_axis=list(),x_axis=list(),annotations=list(), margin=list(t=70,b=90),note_y=-0.16,...) { note<-list(text=paste("Source:",source),xref="paper",yref="paper",x=0,y=note_y,xanchor="left", yanchor="top",showarrow=FALSE,font=list(size=11,color=dark_gray)) result<-layout(p, title=list(text=title,x=0.02,xanchor="left",y=0.97,yanchor="top"), yaxis=c(list(title=y_title),y_axis), xaxis=c(list(title=""),x_axis), margin=margin, annotations=c(annotations,list(note)), ...) %>% config(displaylogo=FALSE) return(result) } legend_top<-list(orientation="h",x=0,y=1.02,yanchor="bottom") # short labels of numbers number<-function(x) { result<-format(round(x),big.mark=",",trim=TRUE) return(result) } percent<-function(x,digits=0,sign=FALSE) { result<-paste0(ifelse(sign&x>0,"+",""),format(round(x,digits),nsmall=digits,trim=TRUE),"%") return(result) } # a week in words: "15–21 July 2024" week_dates<-function(monday) { sunday<-monday+6 start<-ifelse(format(monday,"%m")==format(sunday,"%m"),format(monday,"%e"), format(monday,"%e %B")) result<-paste0(trimws(start),"–",trimws(format(sunday,"%e %B %Y"))) return(result) } ordinal<-function(n) { suffix<-ifelse(n%%100%in%11:13,"th",c("th","st","nd","rd",rep("th",6))[n%%10+1]) result<-paste0(n,suffix) return(result) } ``` ::: --- ## 1. How many people die in Greece in a normal week? **About 2,340.** In 2015–2019 Greece recorded 121,669 deaths in a year of 52 weeks. The worst weeks of a normal year come in winter, with flu and the cold: for a week of January the model expects about 3,020 deaths, for a week of September about 2,020. And as the population ages, the expected deaths grow by about 0.8% a year. --- ## 2. How many more died during the pandemic? **About 38,400 in 2020–2022**, 10% more than a normal three years would have brought. The worst year was 2021, with 18,380 deaths more than expected (+15%). In the chart, the gray band is the range in which a normal week falls; the red line is what happened. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_ly(weekly,x=~monday) %>% add_trace(y=~high,type="scatter",mode="lines",line=list(width=0),hoverinfo="skip", showlegend=FALSE) %>% add_trace(y=~low,type="scatter",mode="lines",line=list(width=0),fill="tonexty", fillcolor="rgba(158,158,158,0.3)",name="Normal range",hoverinfo="skip") %>% add_trace(y=~expected,type="scatter",mode="lines",name="Expected", line=list(color=dark_gray,width=1,dash="dot"), hovertemplate="Expected: %{y:,.0f}") %>% add_trace(y=~deaths,type="scatter",mode="lines",name="Deaths", line=list(color=greek_red,width=1.5), hovertemplate="Deaths: %{y:,.0f}") %>% chart("Deaths in Greece every week", paste0("Eurostat, demo_r_mwk_ts, January 2015 to the week of ", week_dates(weekly$monday[nrow(weekly)]),"; expected: the model above"), "Deaths a week",hovermode="x unified", legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=100,b=90),note_y=-0.12) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The same by year. 2026 has 27 weeks so far. 2015 and 2020 had 53 weeks, and so more deaths and more expected deaths than the other years. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_ly(years,x=~year,y=~excess,type="bar", marker=list(color=ifelse(years$excess>0,greek_red,blue)), text=~percent(percent,sign=TRUE),textposition="outside",cliponaxis=FALSE, hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:,.0f} deaths more than expected") %>% chart("Deaths above (+) or below (−) the expected, each year", "Eurostat, demo_r_mwk_ts; the expected deaths from the model above","Deaths", x_axis=list(dtick=1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} knitr::kable(data.frame(year=years$year,weeks=years$weeks,deaths=number(years$deaths), expected=number(years$expected),excess=number(years$excess), percent=percent(years$percent,1,sign=TRUE)), col.names=c("Year","Weeks","Deaths","Expected","Excess","Excess, %"),align="r") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | Year| Weeks| Deaths| Expected| Excess| Excess, %| |----:|-----:|-------:|--------:|------:|---------:| | 2015| 53| 123,324| 122,175| 1,149| +0.9%| | 2016| 52| 118,116| 120,549| -2,433| -2.0%| | 2017| 52| 124,069| 121,482| 2,587| +2.1%| | 2018| 52| 119,952| 122,423| -2,471| -2.0%| | 2019| 52| 124,538| 123,370| 1,168| +0.9%| | 2020| 53| 132,969| 126,978| 5,991| +4.7%| | 2021| 52| 143,668| 125,288| 18,380| +14.7%| | 2022| 52| 140,292| 126,257| 14,035| +11.1%| | 2023| 52| 127,671| 127,235| 436| +0.3%| | 2024| 52| 126,182| 128,220| -2,038| -1.6%| | 2025| 52| 121,566| 129,212| -7,646| -5.9%| | 2026| 27| 64,952| 70,169| -5,217| -7.4%| ::: ::: --- ## 3. Which weeks were the worst? The ten weeks with the most deaths above the expected: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} worst<-weekly[order(-weekly$excess),][1:10,] hot_weeks<-worst$week>=23&worst$week<=39 # June to September knitr::kable(data.frame(week=week_dates(worst$monday),deaths=number(worst$deaths), expected=number(worst$expected), excess=percent(worst$percent,sign=TRUE), heat=paste0(format(round(worst$tmax,1),nsmall=1)," °C")), col.names=c("Week","Deaths","Expected","Excess","Athens, average highest temperature"), align="lrrrr") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Week | Deaths| Expected| Excess| Athens, average highest temperature| |:---------------------------|------:|--------:|------:|-----------------------------------:| |2–8 August 2021 | 3,895| 2,419| +61%| 38.6 °C| |15–21 July 2024 | 3,268| 2,266| +44%| 36.8 °C| |30 November–6 December 2020 | 3,338| 2,425| +38%| 15.3 °C| |23–29 November 2020 | 3,298| 2,390| +38%| 15.9 °C| |6–12 December 2021 | 3,344| 2,443| +37%| 15.7 °C| |25–31 July 2022 | 3,222| 2,370| +36%| 35.2 °C| |28 June–4 July 2021 | 3,154| 2,359| +34%| 35.5 °C| |13–19 December 2021 | 3,293| 2,504| +32%| 9.8 °C| |22–28 November 2021 | 3,174| 2,404| +32%| 17.3 °C| |29 November–5 December 2021 | 3,177| 2,409| +32%| 16.4 °C| ::: ::: 4 of the ten are **summer weeks**, among them the worst of all, 2–8 August 2021: 3,895 people died, 61% more than expected, while Athens averaged 38.6 °C at the hottest hour of each day. The other 6 are weeks of November 2020, November 2021, December 2021, when the waves of the pandemic filled the hospitals. --- ## 4. Does the heat kill too? **Yes.** Every dot of the chart is a week of June to September since 2015: how hot it was in Athens, where more than a third of the people of Greece live, and how many more people died in all of Greece than expected. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summer<-weekly[weekly$week>=23&weekly$week<=39&!is.na(weekly$tmax),] summer$hover<-paste0(week_dates(summer$monday),": ",format(round(summer$tmax,1),nsmall=1), " °C, deaths ",percent(summer$percent,sign=TRUE)) summer$hot<-summer$tmax>=36 plot_ly(summer[!summer$hot,],x=~tmax,y=~percent,type="scatter",mode="markers", name="Other summer weeks",marker=list(color=gray,size=8,opacity=0.7),hovertext=~hover, hovertemplate="%{hovertext}") %>% add_trace(data=summer[summer$hot,],name="Weeks of 36 °C or more", marker=list(color=greek_red,size=10,opacity=1)) %>% chart("Summer weeks: heat in Athens and deaths in Greece", paste("Eurostat, demo_r_mwk_ts; ERA5-Land through Open-Meteo. Weeks 23 to 39 of each", "year (June to September)."),"Deaths above the expected, %", x_axis=list(title="Average of the highest temperatures of the week in Athens, °C"), legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=100,b=110),note_y=-0.22) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summer$band<-cut(summer$tmax,c(-Inf,30,33,36,Inf),right=FALSE, labels=c("Under 30 °C","30 to 33 °C","33 to 36 °C","36 °C or more")) bands<-aggregate(percent~band,summer,mean) bands$weeks<-as.vector(table(summer$band)[as.character(bands$band)]) knitr::kable(data.frame(band=bands$band,weeks=bands$weeks, excess=percent(bands$percent,1,sign=TRUE)), col.names=c("Athens, average highest temperature of the week","Weeks", "Deaths above the expected, on average"),align="lrr") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Athens, average highest temperature of the week | Weeks| Deaths above the expected, on average| |:-----------------------------------------------|-----:|-------------------------------------:| |Under 30 °C | 47| +0.3%| |30 to 33 °C | 81| +0.6%| |33 to 36 °C | 54| +6.5%| |36 °C or more | 10| +22.4%| ::: ::: In the summer weeks under 33 °C, about as many people died as expected. In the 10 weeks of 36 °C or more, 22% more died than expected, on average. Heat strains the heart and the lungs, most of all in old and sick people (see [Athens Is Getting Hotter](ILLUSTRATION_ATHENS_HEAT.Rmd)). Not every hot week was deadly, though: in the hottest week of all, 21–27 July 2025 at 38.7 °C, deaths were +1% against the expected. --- ## 5. Who died? The same model, fitted to each age group, gives the excess deaths of 2020–2022 by age. The youngest groups are put together, as they have few deaths. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} groups<-list(`Under 40`=c("Y_LT10","Y10-19","Y20-29","Y30-39"),`40–49`="Y40-49", `50–59`="Y50-59",`60–69`="Y60-69",`70–79`="Y70-79",`80–89`="Y80-89", `90 and over`="Y_GE90") ages<-do.call(rbind,lapply(names(groups),function(group) { parts<-lapply(groups[[group]],function(code) { x<-by_age[by_age$age==code,c("time","values")] names(x)[2]<-"deaths" x$year<-as.integer(substr(x$time,1,4)) x$week<-as.integer(substr(x$time,7,8)) expect(x)$weeks }) y<-do.call(rbind,parts) y<-y[y$year%in%2020:2022,] data.frame(age=group,deaths=sum(y$deaths),expected=sum(y$expected)) })) ages$excess<-ages$deaths-ages$expected ages$percent<-100*ages$excess/ages$expected ages$age<-factor(ages$age,levels=ages$age) plot_ly(ages,x=~age,y=~percent,type="bar",marker=list(color=greek_red), text=~number(excess),textposition="outside",cliponaxis=FALSE, hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f}% above the expected") %>% chart("Deaths above the expected by age, 2020–2022, %", "Eurostat, demo_r_mwk_10; the model above, for each group. On the bars: the excess deaths.", "% above the expected") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: In numbers, most of the excess deaths were of old people: 25,775 of the 35,606 were of people aged 70 or more. But against what was expected for each age, the pandemic years hit people aged 60 to 79 hardest (+18%), more than those aged 80 or more (+6%), whose deaths are many in any year. The groups add up to a little less than the total of question 2, as each group has a model of its own and a few deaths have no age. --- ## 6. How does Greece compare with the EU? Eurostat publishes its own measure for every country: the deaths of each month against the average of the same month in 2016–2019. It has no trend for the ageing of the population, so it counts a little more excess than the model above. Averaged over the 36 months of 2020–2022: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} eu_name<-c(setNames(eu_countries$name,eu_countries$code),EU27_2020="EU-27") months_2020_2022<-eurostat_excess[eurostat_excess$time>="2020-01"&eurostat_excess$time<="2022-12"& eurostat_excess$geo%in%names(eu_name),] eu<-aggregate(values~geo,months_2020_2022,mean) eu$name<-eu_name[eu$geo] eu<-eu[order(eu$values),] countries<-eu[eu$geo!="EU27_2020",] greece_rank<-match("EL",rev(countries$geo)) plot_ly(eu,x=~values,y=~factor(name,levels=name),type="bar",orientation="h", marker=list(color=ifelse(eu$geo=="EL",greek_red,ifelse(eu$geo=="EU27_2020",blue,gray))), text=~percent(values,1),textposition="outside",cliponaxis=FALSE, hovertemplate="%{y}: %{x:.1f}% more deaths than in 2016–2019") %>% chart("Deaths above 2016–2019, average month of 2020–2022, %", "Eurostat, demo_mexrt: the deaths of each month against the average of 2016–2019", margin=list(l=130,t=70,b=90),note_y=-0.08) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: **About average.** With 13.6% more deaths a month than in 2016–2019, Greece was 10th of the 27 countries, against 13.3% for the EU as a whole. Bulgaria had the most, Sweden the fewest. --- ## 7. What came after the pandemic? **In 2025, 121,566 people died in Greece, against 121,669 in an average year of 2016–2019: about as many, although the population is older.** Eurostat's measure, which compares each month with 2016–2019 and has no trend, averaged -0.1% for Greece in 2025. The model above expects the deaths to grow by 0.8% a year as the population ages, so it counts 7,646 deaths fewer than expected (-5.9%). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} recent<-eurostat_excess[eurostat_excess$geo%in%c("EL","EU27_2020"),] recent$date<-as.Date(paste0(recent$time,"-01")) recent<-recent[order(recent$date),] plot_ly(recent[recent$geo=="EL",],x=~date,y=~values,type="scatter",mode="lines",name="Greece", line=list(color=greek_red,width=2),hovertemplate="Greece: %{y:.1f}%") %>% add_trace(data=recent[recent$geo=="EU27_2020",],name="EU-27",line=list(color=blue,width=2), hovertemplate="EU-27: %{y:.1f}%") %>% chart("Deaths of each month against 2016–2019, %", paste0("Eurostat, demo_mexrt, January 2020 to ", format(max(recent$date),"%B %Y")),"% above (+) or below (−)", hovermode="x unified",legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=100,b=90)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Two things can keep the deaths of the years after a pandemic below the trend: - **Some of the deaths came early.** The pandemic and the heatwaves took the lives of many people who were already very old or very ill. Some of them would have died in the years that followed; as they died earlier, fewer people die in those years. Demographers call this *mortality displacement*. - **The trend of 2015–2019 may not hold.** The model lets the expected deaths grow by 0.8% a year, as they did before the pandemic. If people now live longer than that trend assumes, the expected deaths are too high, and part of the gap is the model's error, not fewer deaths. --- ## Sources - Eurostat: [demo_r_mwk_ts](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/demo_r_mwk_ts/default/table?lang=en) (deaths by week), [demo_r_mwk_10](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/demo_r_mwk_10/default/table?lang=en) (deaths by week and ten-year age group), [demo_mexrt](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/demo_mexrt/default/table?lang=en) (excess mortality by month). - Temperatures: ERA5-Land ([Muñoz-Sabater et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-13-4349-2021)), through the [historical weather API of Open-Meteo](https://open-meteo.com/en/docs/historical-weather-api) ([Zippenfenig 2023](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7970649)), for the point of the grid nearest to the centre of Athens. --- *Rendered with R 4.6.2 · plotly*
